---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk
chapter: "2 (Cyclical Events / Endurance, Tables 104-109)"
topic: aerobic/anaerobic energy-system transfer asymmetry
category: [endurance, energy-systems, transfer, physiology]
confidence: contested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Energy-System Loads Share Many Cardiorespiratory Indices but Not Time-to-Form: Anaerobic-Lactate Work Shortens Entry to Form in Other Loads — the Book States the Alactate/Aerobic Direction Both Ways

**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
claimed "a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate capacity" and titled itself around broad, one-directional aerobic-to-
alactate transfer. The source states close to the opposite for the specific question of
whether aerobic loads help alactate **sports form**, and it also contradicts itself
internally on a related point. Both corrections below.

**1. Aerobic training does not build alactate sports form, and hurts speed.** Right after
counting how many cardiovascular/respiratory **indices** transfer between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate loads (see the counts below), Bondarchuk states plainly: "The first form
of loads (aerobic) does not show an influence on the development of sports form in the
second form of loads. In other words, in the state of sports form development the aerobic
and anaerobic-alactate abilities of the athlete that come into play are not-dependent on
one another (our data)... aerobic work shows negatively on the development of speed
capabilities." (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146, opened as an image to confirm the text layer.)
So the index-transfer counts below describe shared cardiorespiratory adaptation, not
transfer of competitive sports form, which the author explicitly denies for this pair.

**2. Internal contradiction on which load shortens time-to-form between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate — kept visible per the brief, not harmonized, `confidence: contested`.**
Three passages give different answers:
- PDF p. 164, printed p. 147 (discussing Table 106, anaerobic-alactate → anaerobic-lactate):
  "The anaerobic-alactate training loads do not influence the time of entering the state of
  sports form in anaerobic-lactate. At the same time the latter (anaerobic-lactate) shorten
  the amount of time for entering into the given state in the first form of loads
  (anaerobic-alactate)." This passage is about alactate/lactate, not aerobic/alactate.
- PDF p. 165, printed p. 148 (closing the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate discussion, table 109):
  "Anaerobic-alactate training loads shorten the amount of time of entering into a state of
  sports form in the aerobic exercises. At this time the latter appear to be inert in
  comparison to the first."
- PDF p. 173, printed p. 156: "It was found that anaerobic-lactate loads shorten the time
  for entering into the sports form state in aerobic and anaerobic-alactate. At this time,
  the latter do not influence (do not shorten) the amount of time taken to enter the given
  state in the anaerobic-lactate training loads."
PDF p. 165 says **anaerobic-alactate** shortens aerobic's time-to-form; PDF p. 173 says it
is **anaerobic-lactate** that shortens both aerobic's and anaerobic-alactate's time-to-form.
These cannot both be the full picture. Do not resolve this silently; treat both statements
as the book's own record and cite both locators whenever citing either.

**Index-transfer counts (cardiorespiratory and related indices, not sports-form transfer):**
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: "6 of 7" cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices
  are "fully transferable" (Table 104, PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable:
  blood-lactate level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with
  different fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers
  in anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: "of the 16 tests looked at, only four were
  non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: "non-transferable factors here are all the remaining
  factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147), attributed to the
  oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus the oxygen-dependent
  structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: Table 107's data show the anaerobic-lactate
  loads "bring about much greater functional shifts in the corresponding body systems than
  the anaerobic-alactate, even though the same (white) muscle fibers participate," and "the
  first form of work [anaerobic-lactate] shortens the time period for entering into the
  state of sports form in the second form of loads [anaerobic-alactate]" — the author adds
  "It is not known why." (Table 107, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147.) This is a one-way
  shortening effect (lactate → alactate), not a "also limited" finding.
- Table 106's own printed title reads "Aerobic-Alactate... to the Aerobic-Lactate" (PDF
  p. 168, printed p. 151) — a source typo to note, not a transcription error in this entry.

Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of well-combined aerobic/anaerobic training:
"S. Auita" (**Inference:** almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held world records
simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within tenths of a
second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional career bests:
200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11. (PDF p. 172,
printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation for the index-transfer pattern is
fiber-type recruitment: aerobic training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers,
while anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch)
fibers. He states plainly for the alactate→alactate asymmetry that "it is not known why"
one direction shortens time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed
p. 147) — the author himself flags this as an open question. No mechanism is given for the
aerobic/anaerobic-alactate sports-form independence in point 1 above, or for the internal
contradiction in point 2. Do not read a fuller physiological explanation into this than the
fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this entry as a caution against assuming energy-system training
transfers to competitive sports form the way shared physiological indices might suggest.
Bondarchuk's own data: aerobic loads did not influence anaerobic-alactate sports form, and
aerobic work hurt speed development (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146). Do not use this entry to
support "a block of aerobic work builds a base for alactate capacity" — the author states
the opposite for sports-form transfer specifically, even though many cardiorespiratory
indices are shared. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all three energy
systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target the intended
adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`). **Inference:** this
entry's asymmetry and contradiction findings complicate any simple version of that general
principle for the aerobic/alactate pair specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is contested**: the source itself states the direction
of the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate/anaerobic-lactate time-to-form relationship differently
at PDF p. 165 (printed p. 148) versus PDF p. 173 (printed p. 156); see point 2 above. Do
not silently pick one side. **Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a
single named-athlete case offered as illustration, not independent evidence. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — no football or
team-sport population appears anywhere in this book. The specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards.

**Example** — **Inference:** a program that substitutes heavy sprint/power
("anaerobic-alactate") conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build
aerobic capacity, is not supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices
showed no transfer in that direction. The reverse claim — that aerobic work builds a base
for anaerobic-alactate sports form — is directly contradicted by the author's own PDF
p. 163 statement (point 1 above), even though the shared-index count (Table 104) might
suggest otherwise; do not conflate index overlap with sports-form transfer.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer

# Energy-System Loads Share Many Cardiorespiratory Indices but Not Time-to-Form: Anaerobic-Lactate Work Shortens Entry to Form in Other Loads — the Book States the Alactate/Aerobic Direction Both Ways

**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
claimed "a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate capacity" and titled itself around broad, one-directional aerobic-to-
alactate transfer. The source states close to the opposite for the specific question of
whether aerobic loads help alactate **sports form**, and it also contradicts itself
internally on a related point. Both corrections below.

**1. Aerobic training does not build alactate sports form, and hurts speed.** Right after
counting how many cardiovascular/respiratory **indices** transfer between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate loads (see the counts below), Bondarchuk states plainly: "The first form
of loads (aerobic) does not show an influence on the development of sports form in the
second form of loads. In other words, in the state of sports form development the aerobic
and anaerobic-alactate abilities of the athlete that come into play are not-dependent on
one another (our data)... aerobic work shows negatively on the development of speed
capabilities." (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146, opened as an image to confirm the text layer.)
So the index-transfer counts below describe shared cardiorespiratory adaptation, not
transfer of competitive sports form, which the author explicitly denies for this pair.

**2. Internal contradiction on which load shortens time-to-form between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate — kept visible per the brief, not harmonized, `confidence: contested`.**
Three passages give different answers:
- PDF p. 164, printed p. 147 (discussing Table 106, anaerobic-alactate → anaerobic-lactate):
  "The anaerobic-alactate training loads do not influence the time of entering the state of
  sports form in anaerobic-lactate. At the same time the latter (anaerobic-lactate) shorten
  the amount of time for entering into the given state in the first form of loads
  (anaerobic-alactate)." This passage is about alactate/lactate, not aerobic/alactate.
- PDF p. 165, printed p. 148 (closing the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate discussion, table 109):
  "Anaerobic-alactate training loads shorten the amount of time of entering into a state of
  sports form in the aerobic exercises. At this time the latter appear to be inert in
  comparison to the first."
- PDF p. 173, printed p. 156: "It was found that anaerobic-lactate loads shorten the time
  for entering into the sports form state in aerobic and anaerobic-alactate. At this time,
  the latter do not influence (do not shorten) the amount of time taken to enter the given
  state in the anaerobic-lactate training loads."
PDF p. 165 says **anaerobic-alactate** shortens aerobic's time-to-form; PDF p. 173 says it
is **anaerobic-lactate** that shortens both aerobic's and anaerobic-alactate's time-to-form.
These cannot both be the full picture. Do not resolve this silently; treat both statements
as the book's own record and cite both locators whenever citing either.

**Index-transfer counts (cardiorespiratory and related indices, not sports-form transfer):**
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: "6 of 7" cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices
  are "fully transferable" (Table 104, PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable:
  blood-lactate level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with
  different fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers
  in anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: "of the 16 tests looked at, only four were
  non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: "non-transferable factors here are all the remaining
  factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147), attributed to the
  oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus the oxygen-dependent
  structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: Table 107's data show the anaerobic-lactate
  loads "bring about much greater functional shifts in the corresponding body systems than
  the anaerobic-alactate, even though the same (white) muscle fibers participate," and "the
  first form of work [anaerobic-lactate] shortens the time period for entering into the
  state of sports form in the second form of loads [anaerobic-alactate]" — the author adds
  "It is not known why." (Table 107, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147.) This is a one-way
  shortening effect (lactate → alactate), not a "also limited" finding.
- Table 106's own printed title reads "Aerobic-Alactate... to the Aerobic-Lactate" (PDF
  p. 168, printed p. 151) — a source typo to note, not a transcription error in this entry.

Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of well-combined aerobic/anaerobic training:
"S. Auita" (**Inference:** almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held world records
simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within tenths of a
second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional career bests:
200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11. (PDF p. 172,
printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation for the index-transfer pattern is
fiber-type recruitment: aerobic training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers,
while anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch)
fibers. He states plainly for the alactate→alactate asymmetry that "it is not known why"
one direction shortens time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed
p. 147) — the author himself flags this as an open question. No mechanism is given for the
aerobic/anaerobic-alactate sports-form independence in point 1 above, or for the internal
contradiction in point 2. Do not read a fuller physiological explanation into this than the
fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this entry as a caution against assuming energy-system training
transfers to competitive sports form the way shared physiological indices might suggest.
Bondarchuk's own data: aerobic loads did not influence anaerobic-alactate sports form, and
aerobic work hurt speed development (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146). Do not use this entry to
support "a block of aerobic work builds a base for alactate capacity" — the author states
the opposite for sports-form transfer specifically, even though many cardiorespiratory
indices are shared. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all three energy
systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target the intended
adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`). **Inference:** this
entry's asymmetry and contradiction findings complicate any simple version of that general
principle for the aerobic/alactate pair specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is contested**: the source itself states the direction
of the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate/anaerobic-lactate time-to-form relationship differently
at PDF p. 165 (printed p. 148) versus PDF p. 173 (printed p. 156); see point 2 above. Do
not silently pick one side. **Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a
single named-athlete case offered as illustration, not independent evidence. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — no football or
team-sport population appears anywhere in this book. The specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards.

**Example** — **Inference:** a program that substitutes heavy sprint/power
("anaerobic-alactate") conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build
aerobic capacity, is not supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices
showed no transfer in that direction. The reverse claim — that aerobic work builds a base
for anaerobic-alactate sports form — is directly contradicted by the author's own PDF
p. 163 statement (point 1 above), even though the shared-index count (Table 104) might
suggest otherwise; do not conflate index overlap with sports-form transfer.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is — new entry, review's Missing Item 4.** This entry gathers three related
facts about how throwers historically dosed lighter/heavier-implement work, none of which
were captured by the correlational-transfer entry
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] even after that entry's own
review fixes.

**1. The dosing law: correlations peak close to competition weight, not far from it.**
"The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in
cases where the deviations [from the competitive implement weight] was insignificant in
relation to the competitive — from 10-20%." The weakest values in the whole implement-weight
dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the 16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m
level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at the 20-21m level. (PDF p. 115,
printed p. 98.)

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." For most of the 20th century, throwers used mainly the competitive-weight
implement, with lighter/heavier implements used "sporadically and in small volume" —
heavier implements in the fall-winter season, lighter implements immediately before
competition, typically in 4-6 week cycles. "In the last two decades" (relative to this
book's writing) that changed: lighter, heavier, and competitive-weight implement work
together now comprises **30-50% of the total training time** across the yearly cycle. (PDF
p. 114, printed p. 97.) Distance-difference norms for specific implement/weight pairs by
event and sex are given in Tables 35-40 (PDF pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] for the values).

**3. The "throwing boom" overdose warning.** Bondarchuk names a real historical error, not
a hypothetical one: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which
the athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using
lighter or heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example,
some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session."
He dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (i.e., roughly 1968-1980). He states the boom
"produced negative after-effects" and recommends specialists "increase the volume of
training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable amounts in order to
avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." Separately, he notes that in sports
practice "many specialists are already convinced that the use of imitational exercises
without resistance[s], do not have a positive influence on the development of physical
abilities of low as well as high level athletes" — i.e. dropping the implement's weight
entirely (miming the throw) is not a safe substitute either; the dosing problem runs in
both directions. (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why 200-300+ throws per session produced
negative after-effects, or for why the 10-20% weight-deviation band produces the strongest
correlations. **Inference:** both points are consistent with a dose-response reading —
enough load variation to stress the target quality (strength via heavier, speed via
lighter) without drifting so far from the competitive movement's loading that technique or
recovery capacity breaks down — but the author does not state this interpretation himself
in the excerpted text.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
historical caution on both dosing axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from competition
implement modest (per the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming "more extreme is
better," and (b) do not assume "more volume of variable-weight throws is always more
transferable" — the throwing-boom history shows a real, named historical case where
volume (200-500 throws/session) produced negative after-effects, not better transfer.
**Inference:** mapped loosely onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general caution
against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant, not just
implement-weight throws — that generalization is this entry's own, not the author's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); this entry's dosing law describes which correlations
run highest within that already-positive range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The "throwing
boom" is a specific, dated historical episode (roughly 1968-1980) in Soviet-bloc throws
training, not a controlled study; Bondarchuk gives no session count, athlete count, or
comparison-condition data for the "negative after-effects" claim, and he includes his own
record-holding athletes among those who did it, without saying whether or how it affected
their specific results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for a different
sport's variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer throwing program that rotates through implements
7.26kg (competition), 6kg, and 8kg (roughly 10-17% off competition weight) is better
supported by the dosing law above than one that jumps straight to 16kg or a bare-bar
imitation throw; and a coach programming 200+ standing throws in a single session, echoing
the historical "throwing boom," should treat that volume as a documented historical
cautionary case, not a target.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
correlational finding this entry's dosing law and overdose warning were missing from.
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] — Tables 35-40's specific
distance-difference norms by implement/weight pair. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]
— this book folder's Method paragraph (questionnaires, four Olympic cycles, 0.349
threshold, steroid exclusion), which this entry's dosing-law correlations also fall under.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary quote is broader
in scope than "lighter/heavier vs. competitive": "there is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115) — i.e. it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter/heavier/competitive throws, not
only the lighter/heavier-vs.-competitive pairing this entry's title highlights. He gives
**three** exceptions, not two: javelin, no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and
the 3-4kg standing throw; javelin, no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements;
and, in women, "no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive
implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**The dose that produces the strongest correlations.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
[from competition weight] was insignificant in relation to the competitive — from 10-20%."
The weakest values in the whole dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the
16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at
the 20-21m level — notably, that 0.365 weak value sits at the *top* competitive level, not
a low one, so "near-universal transfer" should carry that qualifier. (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98.) **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the
0.365 value above only barely clears it.

He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125, not PDF
pp. 130-131 as an earlier draft of this entry cited). The same passage contrasts this with
his *specialized-preparatory* exercise results, which tracked the competitive result in
only 8 of 35 cases and were "autonomous" (untracking) in the other 27 — a sharp difference
from the implement-weight throws' near-lockstep pattern (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125).
Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his implement-weight throws
increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances (Table 88, PDF p. 141,
printed p. 124), against his specialized-preparatory exercises tracking in only 32 of 49
instances (32 with, 17 without) (PDF p. 141, printed p. 124) — the same implement-weight-
vs.-specialized-preparatory contrast Sedikh's data shows.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as the strongest, most consistent transfer
finding in the excerpted chapters — for throwing events specifically, varying implement
weight while keeping the competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training
method across nearly the full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any
strength, jump, or sprint assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter — but that
cross-chapter comparison is this entry's own judgment, not a claim the author makes; his
own claim is narrower: "throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to be the most
transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98), without comparing
across chapters. He does flag a real caveat: heavier implements can degrade technique
(release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect he says clears up "in several
weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the double-effect pattern named in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa individual case data (Tables 85-88) is
**untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not as
independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of
mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport (the case-study athletes are elite Soviet-bloc Olympic/world
champions specifically). This finding is specific to implements that can be made lighter
or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact (shot, discus, javelin,
hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight manipulation in most football
skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement identical" as a general
training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a quarterback) is
Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of
5-6 different implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight, ideally
within the 10-20% band shown to correlate most strongly) targeting both speed and strength
qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as a
transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat. [[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]
— the historical dosing/volume data (10-20% deviation band, the "throwing boom" overdose
case) this entry's correlational finding does not itself cover.
====
Transfer of Physical Abilities in the Throws with the 
Use of Different Types of Exercises 
 
The core of the training system for throwers appears to be, that over the duration of the 
yearly cycle, the athletes use a sufficiently large number of exercises repeating the basic 
movement in lighter and more difficult conditions --- i.e., using implements having 
different weights.  The deviation range when using lighter and heavier implements in 
comparison to the competitive implement weight, can vary from several percent to the 
tens and even hundreds of percent.   
 
It is generally known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used 
and for speed, lighter.  In the last two decades the total training loads used in the year-
round training cycle with the use of lighter, heavier and competitive weight implements 
varied between 30-50% of the total amount of time used for training.   
 
In the last 50-60 years in the past century, athletes basically used the competitive weight 
implement.  Heavier and lighter implements were used sporadically and in small volume.  
It was thought that heavier implements should be used in the fall-winter season and 
lighter weights-should be included in the training immediately before the beginning of 
competition.  Usually the heavier and lighter implements were used during 4-6 week 
cycles. 
 
Literary sources which touch on the study of this problem [18, 33, 265, 266] testify to the 
positive influence of lighter and heavier implements on an increase in sports 
achievements in the basic throws.  It was correctly noted that heavier implements can 
have a positive influence on an increase in physical abilities and a negative one on

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is — new entry, review's Missing Item 4.** This entry gathers three related
facts about how throwers historically dosed lighter/heavier-implement work, none of which
were captured by the correlational-transfer entry
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] even after that entry's own
review fixes.

**1. The dosing law: correlations peak close to competition weight, not far from it.**
"The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in
cases where the deviations [from the competitive implement weight] was insignificant in
relation to the competitive — from 10-20%." The weakest values in the whole implement-weight
dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the 16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m
level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at the 20-21m level. (PDF p. 115,
printed p. 98.)

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." For most of the 20th century, throwers used mainly the competitive-weight
implement, with lighter/heavier implements used "sporadically and in small volume" —
heavier implements in the fall-winter season, lighter implements immediately before
competition, typically in 4-6 week cycles. "In the last two decades" (relative to this
book's writing) that changed: lighter, heavier, and competitive-weight implement work
together now comprises **30-50% of the total training time** across the yearly cycle. (PDF
p. 114, printed p. 97.) Distance-difference norms for specific implement/weight pairs by
event and sex are given in Tables 35-40 (PDF pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] for the values).

**3. The "throwing boom" overdose warning.** Bondarchuk names a real historical error, not
a hypothetical one: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which
the athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using
lighter or heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example,
some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session."
He dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (i.e., roughly 1968-1980). He states the boom
"produced negative after-effects" and recommends specialists "increase the volume of
training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable amounts in order to
avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." Separately, he notes that in sports
practice "many specialists are already convinced that the use of imitational exercises
without resistance[s], do not have a positive influence on the development of physical
abilities of low as well as high level athletes" — i.e. dropping the implement's weight
entirely (miming the throw) is not a safe substitute either; the dosing problem runs in
both directions. (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why 200-300+ throws per session produced
negative after-effects, or for why the 10-20% weight-deviation band produces the strongest
correlations. **Inference:** both points are consistent with a dose-response reading —
enough load variation to stress the target quality (strength via heavier, speed via
lighter) without drifting so far from the competitive movement's loading that technique or
recovery capacity breaks down — but the author does not state this interpretation himself
in the excerpted text.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
historical caution on both dosing axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from competition
implement modest (per the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming "more extreme is
better," and (b) do not assume "more volume of variable-weight throws is always more
transferable" — the throwing-boom history shows a real, named historical case where
volume (200-500 throws/session) produced negative after-effects, not better transfer.
**Inference:** mapped loosely onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general caution
against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant, not just
implement-weight throws — that generalization is this entry's own, not the author's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); this entry's dosing law describes which correlations
run highest within that already-positive range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The "throwing
boom" is a specific, dated historical episode (roughly 1968-1980) in Soviet-bloc throws
training, not a controlled study; Bondarchuk gives no session count, athlete count, or
comparison-condition data for the "negative after-effects" claim, and he includes his own
record-holding athletes among those who did it, without saying whether or how it affected
their specific results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for a different
sport's variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer throwing program that rotates through implements
7.26kg (competition), 6kg, and 8kg (roughly 10-17% off competition weight) is better
supported by the dosing law above than one that jumps straight to 16kg or a bare-bar
imitation throw; and a coach programming 200+ standing throws in a single session, echoing
the historical "throwing boom," should treat that volume as a documented historical
cautionary case, not a target.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
correlational finding this entry's dosing law and overdose warning were missing from.
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] — Tables 35-40's specific
distance-difference norms by implement/weight pair. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]
— this book folder's Method paragraph (questionnaires, four Olympic cycles, 0.349
threshold, steroid exclusion), which this entry's dosing-law correlations also fall under.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary quote is broader
in scope than "lighter/heavier vs. competitive": "there is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115) — i.e. it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter/heavier/competitive throws, not
only the lighter/heavier-vs.-competitive pairing this entry's title highlights. He gives
**three** exceptions, not two: javelin, no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and
the 3-4kg standing throw; javelin, no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements;
and, in women, "no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive
implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**The dose that produces the strongest correlations.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
[from competition weight] was insignificant in relation to the competitive — from 10-20%."
The weakest values in the whole dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the
16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at
the 20-21m level — notably, that 0.365 weak value sits at the *top* competitive level, not
a low one, so "near-universal transfer" should carry that qualifier. (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98.) **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the
0.365 value above only barely clears it.

He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125, not PDF
pp. 130-131 as an earlier draft of this entry cited). The same passage contrasts this with
his *specialized-preparatory* exercise results, which tracked the competitive result in
only 8 of 35 cases and were "autonomous" (untracking) in the other 27 — a sharp difference
from the implement-weight throws' near-lockstep pattern (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125).
Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his implement-weight throws
increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances (Table 88, PDF p. 141,
printed p. 124), against his specialized-preparatory exercises tracking in only 32 of 49
instances (32 with, 17 without) (PDF p. 141, printed p. 124) — the same implement-weight-
vs.-specialized-preparatory contrast Sedikh's data shows.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as the strongest, most consistent transfer
finding in the excerpted chapters — for throwing events specifically, varying implement
weight while keeping the competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training
method across nearly the full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any
strength, jump, or sprint assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter — but that
cross-chapter comparison is this entry's own judgment, not a claim the author makes; his
own claim is narrower: "throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to be the most
transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98), without comparing
across chapters. He does flag a real caveat: heavier implements can degrade technique

This double edged inter-effect between lighter, heavier and competitive weight

with great precision, within several percent, to determine the level of achievement in 
other exercises.  For example, two-time Olympic hammer throw champion Yu. Sedikh, 
appears not only as the official world record holder in the throw of the competitive 
implement (86.74m), but unofficially in the throws of two lighter (5 and 6kg) and three 
heavier (8, 9, and 10kg) weights.  We will take note that he was for several years, the 
possessor of the world record in throwing a weight of 16kg---23.90m (tables 85-86).

in the throw of the implement weighting of 6, 8, and 10kg.  In his time, he established the 
world record in the competitive throws three times.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
113 
 
And still another example is related to the training of women.  Olympic champion in the 
shotput N. Lisovskaya, was the official world record holder in the throw of the 
competitive implement and unofficial in the throw of the 3, 7, 5 and 6kg shot.  Similar 
examples exist in other track and field throw events.

developmental exercises (throws and “shot putting” various implements having different 
weights from place) and exercises with lighter, heavier and competitive implements.  The 
amounts of these interrelationships are sufficiently great (see tables 69-84).  There is no 
relationship in only two places out of the many.  In javelin throwers, no positive 
interrelationship is observed between throws of a lighter implement weighing 0.6kg and 
throws of a heavier implement weighing 3 and 4 kg from place.  There is also no 
interrelationship between throws with a lighter implement weighing 0.7kg and heavier 
ones weighing 4kg. 
 
In the women, there is no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the 
competitive implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg.  Here once 
again as between the lighter, heavier and competitive weight exercises, there is a tight 
interrelationship between knowing the result in the throws from place, and making an 
early prognosis of sports achievement in the entire throw.  Also the opposite, at a definite 
level of sports achievement in the competitive exercise, there exists a definite level of 
results in the throw from place.   
 
In sports practice, in each track and field throw event, a specific number of specialized 
developmental exercises are used, mainly throws of the implement of various weights 
from place starting in various positions.  To a lesser degree, there are exercises that repeat 
other joint parts of the total competitive movement.  Discussion here is related mainly to 
the throwing steps taken by the javelin thrower, the turns by the hammer and discus 
thrower, and glides or skips by shotputters.  It appears to us that in the future, their 
portion of the total volume of training loads will increase somewhat.

Regarding the interrelationship between indices in the throws of lighter, heavier and 
competitive weight implements, an increase or decrease in results in one of them leads to 
an adequate change in the other as seen in the data put together in table 86.  Of them, we 
can see that in Olympic champion Yu. Sedikh, that in 35 instances with a change in the 
test results in the lighter and heavier implements there was a corresponding change in the 
throw of the competitive weight.  In only three instances did the results increase or

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is** — Three related points about how throwers dose lighter and
heavier implement work. The correlational finding itself (lighter and heavier implement
throws transfer to the competitive throw at nearly every level) is in
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]; this entry holds the dosing
detail.

**1. Correlations run highest close to competition weight.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
between the lighter and heavier implement weights was insignificant in relation to the
competitive", and the source continues: "from 10-20%." The author then names the two
lowest values: "The smallest correlation was fixed in the hammer throw when athletes had
results in the at 60-65m range when throwing the 16kg weight (0.425). A weak
interrelationship (0.365) was observed between results in the shotput with weights of 5.0
and 7.260 kg in athletes throwing the shot 20-21m." (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98.)
**Inference:** both of those pairs are far from competition weight (the 16kg weight against
the 7.26kg hammer; the 5.0kg against the 7.260kg shot), which fits the 10-20% statement,
but the author lists the two values without linking them to deviation size.

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." "In the last 50-60 years in the past century, athletes basically used the
competitive weight implement. Heavier and lighter implements were used sporadically and in
small volume." Heavier implements were thought to belong in the fall-winter season and
lighter ones immediately before competition, "Usually ... during 4-6 week cycles." "In the
last two decades" (relative to the book's writing) lighter, heavier and competitive-weight
implement work together "varied between 30-50% of the total amount of time used for
training." (PDF p. 114, printed p. 97.) The author also notes that heavier implements can
help physical abilities and hurt technical mastery [18, 152] (PDF p. 114). Distance-difference
norms for specific implement and weight pairs by event and sex are in Tables 35-40 (PDF
pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see [[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]]).

**3. The "throwing boom" warning.** Bondarchuk reports what specialists recommend: "For
development of speed-strength abilities of the legs, specialists recommend an increase in
the volume of training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable
amounts in order to avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." He then names the
error: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which the athletes
in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using lighter or
heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example, some
hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session." He
dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (**Inference:** roughly 1968 to 1980). His own
generalisation follows: "We did not want to witness the 'imitational' or 'turn-skip'
booms. There should be an optimal amount everywhere or the after-effect will be fraught
with negative consequences." On the same page he reports that "many specialists are
already convinced that the use of imitational exercises without resistance, do not have a
positive influence on the development of physical abilities of low as well as high level
athletes." (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.) **Inference:** read together, too much
variable-weight volume and no resistance at all are both warned against, so the dosing
problem runs in both directions.

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for why the 10-20% band correlates most
strongly, and none for the "negative consequences" of excess volume. For the implement
throws in general he says they are "identical to themselves according to the basic
parameters beginning with the technical and rhythmical composition" (PDF p. 115).
**Inference:** both points fit a dose-response reading (enough load variation to stress
strength via heavier or speed via lighter implements, without drifting so far from the
competitive loading that technique or recovery breaks down), but the author does not state
this.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
caution on two axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from the competition implement modest
(the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming a larger deviation is better, and (b) do not
assume more volume of variable-weight throws is always better; the author calls the
200-500-throws-per-session era an error and warns of "negative consequences" without an
"optimal amount". **Inference:** mapped onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general
caution against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant. That
generalisation is this entry's, though the author's own "optimal amount everywhere"
sentence points the same way.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence:** `supported` for the 10-20% correlation pattern
(PDF p. 115); `untested` for the throwing-boom account (PDF p. 133), a single uncontrolled
historical episode. **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed
p. 59); the dosing statement describes which correlations run highest within the positive
range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and
field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic
cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed
p. 59); not football, not team sport. The throwing boom concerns track and field throwers
(the author names his own record holders among them); it is a dated historical episode,
not a study. Bondarchuk gives no athlete count, no comparison condition and no measured
outcome for the "negative consequences", and he does not say how the boom affected his own
athletes' results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for another sport's
variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer program that rotates the 7.26kg competition hammer
with 6kg and 8kg implements (roughly 17% lighter and 10% heavier) is better supported by
the 10-20% statement than one that jumps straight to the 16kg weight or to an imitation
throw with no implement; and a coach planning 200+ standing throws in one session, as in
the throwing boom, should treat that volume as the author's documented error, not a
target.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]: the
correlational finding this dosing detail belongs to.
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]]: Tables 35-40's
distance-difference norms by implement and weight pair.
[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]: this book folder's Method
paragraph (questionnaires, four Olympic cycles, 0.349 threshold, steroid exclusion), which
these correlations also fall under.

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is — new entry, review's Missing Item 4.** This entry gathers three related
facts about how throwers historically dosed lighter/heavier-implement work, none of which
were captured by the correlational-transfer entry
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] even after that entry's own
review fixes.

**1. The dosing law: correlations peak close to competition weight, not far from it.**
"The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in
cases where the deviations [from the competitive implement weight] was insignificant in
relation to the competitive — from 10-20%." The weakest values in the whole implement-weight
dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the 16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m
level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at the 20-21m level. (PDF p. 115,
printed p. 98.)

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." For most of the 20th century, throwers used mainly the competitive-weight
implement, with lighter/heavier implements used "sporadically and in small volume" —
heavier implements in the fall-winter season, lighter implements immediately before
competition, typically in 4-6 week cycles. "In the last two decades" (relative to this
book's writing) that changed: lighter, heavier, and competitive-weight implement work
together now comprises **30-50% of the total training time** across the yearly cycle. (PDF
p. 114, printed p. 97.) Distance-difference norms for specific implement/weight pairs by
event and sex are given in Tables 35-40 (PDF pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] for the values).

**3. The "throwing boom" overdose warning.** Bondarchuk names a real historical error, not
a hypothetical one: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which
the athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using
lighter or heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example,
some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session."
He dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (i.e., roughly 1968-1980). He states the boom
"produced negative after-effects" and recommends specialists "increase the volume of
training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable amounts in order to
avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." Separately, he notes that in sports
practice "many specialists are already convinced that the use of imitational exercises
without resistance[s], do not have a positive influence on the development of physical
abilities of low as well as high level athletes" — i.e. dropping the implement's weight
entirely (miming the throw) is not a safe substitute either; the dosing problem runs in
both directions. (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why 200-300+ throws per session produced
negative after-effects, or for why the 10-20% weight-deviation band produces the strongest
correlations. **Inference:** both points are consistent with a dose-response reading —
enough load variation to stress the target quality (strength via heavier, speed via
lighter) without drifting so far from the competitive movement's loading that technique or
recovery capacity breaks down — but the author does not state this interpretation himself
in the excerpted text.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
historical caution on both dosing axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from competition
implement modest (per the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming "more extreme is
better," and (b) do not assume "more volume of variable-weight throws is always more
transferable" — the throwing-boom history shows a real, named historical case where
volume (200-500 throws/session) produced negative after-effects, not better transfer.
**Inference:** mapped loosely onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general caution
against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant, not just
implement-weight throws — that generalization is this entry's own, not the author's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); this entry's dosing law describes which correlations
run highest within that already-positive range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The "throwing
boom" is a specific, dated historical episode (roughly 1968-1980) in Soviet-bloc throws
training, not a controlled study; Bondarchuk gives no session count, athlete count, or
comparison-condition data for the "negative after-effects" claim, and he includes his own
record-holding athletes among those who did it, without saying whether or how it affected
their specific results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for a different
sport's variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

7.26kg (competition), 6kg, and 8kg (roughly 10-17% off competition weight) is better
supported by the dosing law above than one that jumps straight to 16kg or a bare-bar
imitation throw; and a coach programming 200+ standing throws in a single session, echoing
the historical "throwing boom," should treat that volume as a documented historical
cautionary case, not a target.

correlational finding this entry's dosing law and overdose warning were missing from.

threshold, steroid exclusion), which this entry's dosing-law correlations also fall under.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter and heavier implements (for example a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer or weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men
and women across shot put, discus, javelin and hammer. The author's summary is broader in
scope than "lighter/heavier against competitive": "There is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115). So it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter, heavier and competitive throws,
not only the pairing this entry's title highlights.

**Exceptions.** The author counts "only two places out of the many" without a
relationship, both in javelin: no positive interrelationship between the 0.6kg implement
and standing throws of 3 and 4kg, and none between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements. The next
paragraph adds a third case, which he does not include in that count: in women, "there is
no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive implement and in
standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**Dosing.** The author finds the strongest correlations where implement weights deviate
from competition weight by only 10-20%, and names the two lowest values, 0.425 (16kg
weight, hammer throwers at 60-65m) and 0.365 (5.0kg against 7.260kg shot, 20-21m throwers)
(PDF p. 115, printed p. 98). The full dosing text is in
[[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]. **A positive
interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the 0.365 value only
barely clears it. **Inference:** 20-21m is a high level of shot putting, so "near-universal
transfer" should carry that qualifier.

**Individual cases.** He illustrates the pattern with elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation). Two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh was the official world record holder with the competitive implement (86.74m)
and "unofficially in the throws of two lighter (5 and 6kg) and three heavier (8, 9, and
10kg) weights", and for several years held the record for the 16kg weight, 23.90m (PDF
p. 130, printed p. 113). His year-by-year data show that "in 35 instances with a change in
the test results in the lighter and heavier implements there was a corresponding change in
the throw of the competitive weight. In only three instances did the results increase or
decrease insignificantly." By contrast, his specialized-preparatory exercise results
matched the competitive result in eight cases "and in only 27 cases were they autonomous"
(PDF p. 142, printed p. 125). Olympic champion R. Yubartasa (the source's spelling) shows
the same contrast over five years: 29 cases where implement throws and the competitive
result rose together against five where they did not, and 32 against 17 for his
specialized-preparatory exercises (Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter and heavier implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98). **Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]],
this is as close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as the book offers (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which fits the transfer factors in
[[framework--transfer-factors-general-to-competitive]]. That classification-based reading
is this entry's, not the author's.

**When to apply** — The author's own claim: "throws with lighter and heavier implements
appear to be the most transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98). **Inference:** for throwing events, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact looks like the most consistent transfer finding in the
excerpted chapters, more consistent than the strength, jump or sprint assistance exercises
tested elsewhere in Chapter 2. That cross-event comparison is this entry's judgment; the
author does not compare across sections. He flags a caveat: heavier implements can change
technique (release angle, trunk lean backward, reduced amplitude), deviations noted by
several authors [18, 152] that "can be eliminated in several weekly cycles" once the
implement is dropped (PDF p. 115). This is the double-effect pattern in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh and Yubartasa individual case data (Tables 85-88)
is **untested**: single elite-athlete cases presented as illustration, not as independent
evidence, and Bondarchuk frames them as examples ("It is possible to bring in many similar
examples from sports practice", PDF p. 142). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign
track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The case-study athletes are Olympic
champions. The finding is specific to implements that can be made lighter or heavier while
keeping the throwing motion intact (shot, discus, javelin, hammer); most football skills
have no direct equivalent, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement identical"
to football (for example weighted-ball throwing for a quarterback) is Inference by
analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer thrower's plan built around a rotation of several
implement weights, lighter and heavier than competition weight and mostly within the
10-20% band, is better supported by this data as a transfer method than substituting
generic barbell strength work for the same purpose (see
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]: the classification behind
this exercise's high transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]: the much
more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same events.
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]]: the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat. [[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]:
the dosing detail (10-20% band, historical practice, the "throwing boom").

from competition weight by only 10-20%, and names the two lowest values, 0.425 (16kg
weight, hammer throwers at 60-65m) and 0.365 (5.0kg against 7.260kg shot, 20-21m throwers)
(PDF p. 115, printed p. 98). The full dosing text is in
[[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]. **A positive
interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the 0.365 value only
barely clears it. **Inference:** 20-21m is a high level of shot putting, so "near-universal
transfer" should carry that qualifier.

**Individual cases.** He illustrates the pattern with elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation). Two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh was the official world record holder with the competitive implement (86.74m)
and "unofficially in the throws of two lighter (5 and 6kg) and three heavier (8, 9, and
10kg) weights", and for several years held the record for the 16kg weight, 23.90m (PDF
p. 130, printed p. 113). His year-by-year data show that "in 35 instances with a change in
the test results in the lighter and heavier implements there was a corresponding change in
the throw of the competitive weight. In only three instances did the results increase or
decrease insignificantly." By contrast, his specialized-preparatory exercise results
matched the competitive result in eight cases "and in only 27 cases were they autonomous"
(PDF p. 142, printed p. 125). Olympic champion R. Yubartasa (the source's spelling) shows
the same contrast over five years: 29 cases where implement throws and the competitive
result rose together against five where they did not, and 32 against 17 for his
specialized-preparatory exercises (Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter and heavier implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98). **Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]],
this is as close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as the book offers (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which fits the transfer factors in
[[framework--transfer-factors-general-to-competitive]]. That classification-based reading
is this entry's, not the author's.

**When to apply** — The author's own claim: "throws with lighter and heavier implements
appear to be the most transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98). **Inference:** for throwing events, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact looks like the most consistent transfer finding in the
excerpted chapters, more consistent than the strength, jump or sprint assistance exercises
tested elsewhere in Chapter 2. That cross-event comparison is this entry's judgment; the
author does not compare across sections. He flags a caveat: heavier implements can change
technique (release angle, trunk lean backward, reduced amplitude), deviations noted by
several authors [18, 152] that "can be eliminated in several weekly cycles" once the
implement is dropped (PDF p. 115). This is the double-effect pattern in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh and Yubartasa individual case data (Tables 85-88)
is **untested**: single elite-athlete cases presented as illustration, not as independent
evidence, and Bondarchuk frames them as examples ("It is possible to bring in many similar
examples from sports practice", PDF p. 142). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign
track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The case-study athletes are Olympic
champions. The finding is specific to implements that can be made lighter or heavier while
keeping the throwing motion intact (shot, discus, javelin, hammer); most football skills
have no direct equivalent, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement identical"
to football (for example weighted-ball throwing for a quarterback) is Inference by
analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer thrower's plan built around a rotation of several
implement weights, lighter and heavier than competition weight and mostly within the
10-20% band, is better supported by this data as a transfer method than substituting
generic barbell strength work for the same purpose (see
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]: the classification behind
this exercise's high transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]: the much
more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same events.
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]]: the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat. [[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]:
the dosing detail (10-20% band, historical practice, the "throwing boom").

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw **in most event/sex groups** (exception: javelin, see
below), but **only up to a specific result level for each exercise and event**, after
which the correlation with further competitive improvement disappears. Worked examples
with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m (men) / 55-60m (women); power
clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m
(women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's
cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three. In shot put, snatch ended at
17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m (men)/14-25m (women — a probable typo
in the printed text, not an OCR artifact: the source PDF has a real text layer, not a
scanned/OCR'd page, so this is either a source misprint or an unusually wide band), squat
at 19-20m (men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). **In javelin, the
"all four transfer" pattern breaks**: snatch and power clean both ended at 65-70m (men);
at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for either the squat or the bench
press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat
"showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135, printed pp. 116-118.)
Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the close of this chapter:
"specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in the sports
result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery. Further on, they
do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He also notes, from the same
chapter's closing material, that "the leading throwers (world and Olympic champions and
world record holders) do not always have the best absolute results in the specialized-
preparatory exercises" (PDF p. 139, printed p. 122) — a further data point supporting the
ceiling: being the best thrower does not require the best strength numbers.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
