# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing, but Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin and hammer, Bondarchuk tests four
strength exercises: snatch, power clean, squat with the barbell on the shoulders, and
bench press. Hammer throwers are the exception for the bench press, "as this exercise is
not used by most of them in the process of training" (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116). The
exercises show a positive transfer to the competitive throw **in most event and sex
groups** (exception: javelin, see below), but **only up to a specific result level for
each exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive
improvement disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer was
observed up to 45-50m (men) and 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m;
bench press extended furthest, to 55-60m (men) and 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch
reached 60-65m, power clean 65-70m, squat 60-65m (men); in women, the cumulative effect
was fixed "at the level of 45-60m" for these exercises (women throw the 4kg hammer, so
these distances are not comparable with the men's 7.26kg distances). In shot put, snatch
reached 17-18m (men) and 15-16m (women), power clean 14-15m (men) and "14-25m" (women; a
probable typo in the printed text, since the source has a real text layer rather than
OCR, so this is either a source misprint or an unusually wide band), squat 19-20m (men)
and 17-18m (women), bench 18-19m (men) and 19-20m (women). **In javelin, the pattern
breaks**: snatch and power clean both reached 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was
no correlation seen" for either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch reached
60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, and the squat showed "no cumulative transfer
effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-134, printed pp. 116-117.)

**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the result
levels above are the qualification bands where the correlations clear that threshold.

Bondarchuk's aggregate summary at the close of the book's data chapters:
"specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in the sports
result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery. Further on, they
do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) Later in the same throws
section he adds that "the leading throwers (world and Olympic champions and world record
holders) do not always have the best absolute results in the specialized-preparatory
exercises" (PDF p. 139, printed p. 122). **Inference:** this fits the ceiling: being the
best thrower does not require the best strength numbers.

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for why the ceiling occurs at these
levels. **Inference:** it is consistent with a diminishing-returns pattern: general
strength predicts performance at lower levels of mastery, but once strength is no longer
the limiting factor, technical and specialized qualities (captured better by the
specialized-developmental exercises in
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) become the binding
constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this interpretation.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a thrower's (or other power athlete's)
emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward specialized-developmental
work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the athlete's **competitive
result** passes the band where the cumulative effect ends for their event (the ceilings
above are competition-distance bands, not strength-load thresholds), rather than chasing
strength PRs as the main lever for competitive improvement.

author cautions against reading them as fixed for every individual: "if we take into
consideration individual and not group indices in the above mentioned strength exercises,

# In Endurance Events, Correlation Rises as the Training Distance Nears the Race Distance, and the Transfer Range Shifts Longer as Race Distance Grows

**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase in
the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m and
1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase starts from 600m and women's 3000m from 400m; 5000m runners' range starts
around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144). Separately, and stated as a distinct
finding, he adds the book's main correlation-strength regularity for this section: "with a
decrease in the difference between the competitive distances and the test exercises used,
the coefficient of correlation increases" (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144) — the
closer a training segment sits to the race distance, the higher its correlation with the
competitive result tends to run. Elsewhere the same data is described as "with an increase
in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases" (PDF
p. 145, printed p. 128, discussing 800m vs. 1500m runners) and, in the chapter's own
closing summary, "the range of transfer in the short distances in most endurance events is
significantly wider than in the long distances" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144) — both
statements are the author's own, given with their own locators; this entry keeps them side
by side rather than picking one.

Representative correlation values: men's 800m showed its strongest correlations with the
400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912, biggest at 1000m: 0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856;
PDF p. 144, printed p. 127, Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by
3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed positive transfer "on all levels of the segments tested"
except that "transfer to the competitive event from the 100 and 200m runs were
non-existent," strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m (0.725-0.906, Table 99, PDF p. 146, printed
p. 129). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners (and 10km-walk
women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer* than the
competitive distance. The author gives this as two separate sentences, not one
"because"-clause: "In these cases, it is not possible to observe the presence of the
cumulative effect with distances that are longer than the competitive event. In sports
practice similar tests do not exist." (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
**Inference:** one possible reading is that longer events draw on a broader mix of energy
systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of training distances can stress a
physiologically relevant system for that event; this interpretation is this entry's own
reading, not stated by the author, and no outside exercise-physiology source was checked
in this ingest to confirm it.

**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport; the specific segment distances and
correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking segment
distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise transfer to
endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range for longer
events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context (football's
actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is Inference:
football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in the way
every sport in this dataset is.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 10,000m runner's program using training distances from
600m intervals up to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's
transfer-range findings; a marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer
benefit from segments longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to
test or train.

these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
how close the segment is to full race distance).

significantly wider than in the long distances" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144); the book
does not say that longer events require a wider spread. **Eric's

threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`). **Inference:** this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport; the specific segment distances and
correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running and walking segment
distances only**; it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise transfer to
endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range for longer
events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context (football's
actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is Inference:
football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in the way
every sport in this dataset is.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 10,000m runner's program using training distances from
600m intervals up to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's
transfer-range findings; a marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer
benefit from segments longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to
test or train.

these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on

content.content:
**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase in
the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments": 800m and
1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase starts from 600m and women's 3000m from 400m; 5000m runners' range starts
around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women). So the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144). Separately, and stated as a distinct
finding, he adds the book's main correlation-strength regularity for this section: "with a
decrease in the difference between the competitive distances and the test exercises used,
the coefficient of correlation increases" (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144): the
closer a training segment sits to the race distance, the higher its correlation with the
competitive result tends to run. Elsewhere the same data is described as "with an increase
in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases" (PDF
p. 145, printed p. 128, discussing 800m vs. 1500m runners) and, in the chapter's own
closing summary, "the range of transfer in the short distances in most endurance events is
significantly wider than in the long distances" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144). Both
statements are the author's own, given with their own locators; this entry keeps them side
by side rather than picking one.

Representative correlation values: in the 800m the greatest correlations were with the
400m, 600m and 1000m segments, "from 0.700-0.900" in both sexes, and in men the biggest
was with the 1000m (0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856; PDF p. 144, printed p. 127; Table 89, PDF
p. 149). **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59). The
men's 800m range ends with the 5000m run, which "had a place on two levels of sports
mastery" (PDF p. 144); in Table 89 that row runs 0.325, 0.325, 0.376, 0.350, so it clears
0.349 on exactly two levels (PDF p. 149, printed p. 132); women's 3000m showed positive transfer "on all levels of the segments tested"
except that "transfer to the competitive event from the 100 and 200m runs were
non-existent," strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m (0.725-0.906, Table 99, PDF p. 146, printed
p. 129). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners (and 10km-walk
women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer* than the
competitive distance. The author gives this as two separate sentences, not one
"because"-clause: "In these cases, it is not possible to observe the presence of the
cumulative effect with distances that are longer than the competitive event. In sports
practice similar tests do not exist." (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

# Bondarchuk Publishes 40 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification

**What it is** — Tables 1-34 run PDF pp. 44-60, printed pp. 27-43 (this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34); Tables 35-40 plus surrounding
prose run PDF pp. 61-64, printed pp. 44-47 — the section is 40 tables, not 34, and the
last six were not covered by an earlier draft of this entry. Tables 1-34 give normative
"model characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s
vs. 10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) with

# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly (high-qualification/low-qualification):
100m runners' 30m-flying-start correlated 0.678/0.778 with the 30m-from-blocks segment and
0.756/0.876 with the 100m-from-blocks segment (Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles
result correlated only 0.562/0.420 with the 200m-from-blocks segment, the weakest pairing
involving the competitive 110m hurdles result (Table 44 has still-lower pairings among its
other rows, e.g. 30m-from-blocks vs. 150m at 0.390/0.426 and vs. 200m at 0.414/0.361, PDF
p. 81, printed p. 64); 400m hurdlers' 400m-hurdles result correlated as high as
0.890/0.806 with the 600m-from-a-high-start segment (Table 45). **A positive
interrelationship between exercises begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59).

**Why it works** — The tables report the correlations without explaining them. **Inference:**
reading this through
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — these are all specialized-developmental
or competitive-class exercises (shorter/longer runs at or near race intensity), sharing
most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system demands, which would
predict the high correlation observed — but this connection is this entry's own reading,
not a claim the author makes for this specific table set.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`). **Inference:** this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy — that reading is this entry's own extension.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The correlations described are all
between running-based specialized-developmental/competitive exercises — this entry does
NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer, which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m
and 300m repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m
and 300m-to-200m correlations ran 0.707-0.888 / 0.724-0.842), slightly more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) flying segments (0.708-0.730) for that
specific event — a small gap, not a large one.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

specific event — a small gap, not a large one.

the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55 itself at PDF p. 95,
printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's
own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). **Exception:** men's 110m hurdles is not a narrow
band like the others — the snatch's cumulative effect there is "lacking only on two levels
of sports mastery" (16.00-16.60sec and 15.00-15.50sec), i.e. present on most levels (PDF
p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)
**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59).

**Why he chose these two lifts.** Bondarchuk explains why the snatch and half squat were
the strength exercises studied, not an arbitrary pair: they let him evaluate total-body
strength (snatch) and leg-extensor strength (half squat) separately, and "according to
their biomechanical characteristics (direction of movement, consecutiveness of including
muscle groups in the work, regimes of muscle work, and so on) duplicate many strength
exercises that are systematically used in the training process. Knowing the results in
each of these exercises makes it possible to predict achievement in other exercises" (PDF
p. 88, printed p. 71). **Inference:** this entry's own caution — that the poor-transfer
finding "should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise variation without
its own data" — follows from that same passage but is this entry's extension, not a
limitation the author states himself; the author frames the two lifts as broadly
representative, not narrow.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives both readings, not one: "the absence of the
cumulative training effect from the snatch and half squat with the barbell on the
shoulders to the competitive event in the men's and women's 400m hurdles, as well as the
barbell snatch to the 200 and 400m can be interpreted in different ways. In one case, it
indicates the ineffectiveness of the given exercise, while in another, that the positive
transfer is conditioned by the use of other methodological means. This relates primarily
to the number of repetitions in one set, the compactness of the strength training sessions
or their parts, and likewise the zones of intensity used." He closes with a general rule:
"the cumulative effect from strength exercises will appear only when they are close to the
competitive event according to the biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters"
(PDF p. 102, printed p. 85). **Inference:** in the terms this book itself defines, the
snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory exercises (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime — this classification-based
reading is this entry's own, not spelled out by the author in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport; tested with a specific barbell snatch
and a half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or
trap-bar variant). **Inference:** the finding should not be assumed to hold for a
different strength exercise variation without its own data, though the author himself
frames the snatch and half squat as broadly representative of systematically-used strength
exercises (PDF p. 88, printed p. 71), not as narrow or unusual choices. This is track and
field data; extending "barbell strength work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed
past a certain level" to football speed training is Inference. No outside source was
checked in this ingest to confirm whether this pattern holds beyond Bondarchuk's own
dataset; treat it as this book's finding only until cross-checked.

**Example** — **Inference:** a high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should
not expect squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this
data; a developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the
band where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). Women's 10-fold-jump-from-place row in Table 64 is 0.886, 0.965,
0.905, 0.890, 0.865 across the five qualification bands — a range of **0.865-0.965**, not
0.886-0.965 as an earlier draft of this entry stated (taking only the first two values'
span instead of the row's true min/max). The men's 10-fold row (Table 63) is 0.876-0.945.
**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59) throughout this
book; all values cited here clear that threshold.

**High jump and the source's own internal contradiction — kept visible, not resolved.**
Two passages describe high jump's correlations differently, and this entry records both
rather than picking one: PDF p. 112 (printed p. 95) says "in all cases, a weak
interrelationship between the test results was observed on the 0.400 level" for men's and
women's high jump generally. But PDF p. 105 (printed p. 88), describing the same Tables
63-64, says "a correlational interrelationship was observed in all running and jumping
exercises," with jump exercises running much stronger than the running exercises: the
prose there gives the vertical jump with a short run-up (matching the 10-fold-jump row's
values, see the exact-match note below) at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women), and
Tables 63-64's 100m-from-blocks row runs roughly 0.60-0.71 across both sexes — not a
uniform 0.400-level weak relationship. The source contradicts itself on how weak high
jump's correlations actually are; do not resolve it in a future entry without checking
the original Russian or a second translation.

**Note on the 0.876-0.945/0.865-0.965 figures above:** the prose at PDF p. 105 (printed
p. 88) names them "the vertical jump with a short run-up," but those exact figures match
the "10-fold jump from place" row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965; the
women's true range per the row's five values is 0.865-0.965, see above), not the row
literally labeled "Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women
0.680-0.808, which the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may
be a translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's
row label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian
or a second translation.

**Snatch, corrected.** The prior version of this entry said the barbell snatch "showed
almost no transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects." The
source states more transfer than that: for men's pole vault, "a positive transfer was
observed on all levels of sports results in the barbell snatch and in the half squat with
the barbell on the shoulders" (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94); more broadly, "in the second
strength exercise (barbell snatch) the cumulative training effect had a place on several
levels of sports mastery in most events except for the women's high jump and men's triple
jump" (PDF p. 112, printed p. 95). Men's long jump snatch correlations ran 6.5-7.3m level
(PDF p. 103, printed p. 86). The half squat with barbell transferred even more
consistently — all levels, both sexes, in high jump and pole vault (PDF p. 112, printed
p. 95).

**Women's pole vault exception.** The single strongest correlation for women pole vaulters
was not the short-run-up vault: it was the 60m run from blocks (0.856, 0.886), above the
short-run-up vault itself (0.788, 0.865) (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94) — an exception to
"short-run-up is the single strongest exercise across event types" worth carrying alongside
that generalization. (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closer to the competitive event than general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises —
but this connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation, and
the internal high-jump contradiction above shows the pattern is not clean even on the
author's own numbers. **Inference:** the high jump's approach and takeoff (curved run,
back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a straight-line sprint that
raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer "identical elements" with it than
with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches — this technique speculation is this
entry's own; the author does not state which high-jump technique his athletes used.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. **Inference:** the "high jump breaks
the pattern" finding may be specific to whichever high-jump technique (Fosbury flop,
straddle, or other) Bondarchuk's athletes used; the text does not state which technique,
so this is speculation, not a stated limitation. Applying any of these specific exercise
priorities to a football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no
football population data exists in this source.

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). Women's 10-fold-jump-from-place row in Table 64 is 0.886, 0.965,
0.905, 0.890, 0.865 across the five qualification bands — a range of **0.865-0.965**, not
0.886-0.965 as an earlier draft of this entry stated (taking only the first two values'
span instead of the row's true min/max). The men's 10-fold row (Table 63) is 0.876-0.945.
**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59) throughout this
book; all values cited here clear that threshold.

**High jump and the source's own internal contradiction — kept visible, not resolved.**
Two passages describe high jump's correlations differently, and this entry records both
rather than picking one: PDF p. 112 (printed p. 95) says "in all cases, a weak
interrelationship between the test results was observed on the 0.400 level" for men's and
women's high jump generally. But PDF p. 105 (printed p. 88), describing the same Tables
63-64, says "a correlational interrelationship was observed in all running and jumping
exercises," with jump exercises running much stronger than the running exercises: the
prose there gives the vertical jump with a short run-up (matching the 10-fold-jump row's
values, see the exact-match note below) at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women), and
Tables 63-64's 100m-from-blocks row runs roughly 0.60-0.71 across both sexes — not a
uniform 0.400-level weak relationship. The source contradicts itself on how weak high
jump's correlations actually are; do not resolve it in a future entry without checking
the original Russian or a second translation.

**Note on the 0.876-0.945/0.865-0.965 figures above:** the prose at PDF p. 105 (printed
p. 88) names them "the vertical jump with a short run-up," but those exact figures match
the "10-fold jump from place" row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965; the
women's true range per the row's five values is 0.865-0.965, see above), not the row
literally labeled "Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women
0.680-0.808, which the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may
be a translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's
row label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian
or a second translation.

**Snatch, corrected.** The prior version of this entry said the barbell snatch "showed
almost no transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects." The
source states more transfer than that: for men's pole vault, "a positive transfer was
observed on all levels of sports results in the barbell snatch and in the half squat with
the barbell on the shoulders" (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94); more broadly, "in the second
strength exercise (barbell snatch) the cumulative training effect had a place on several
levels of sports mastery in most events except for the women's high jump and men's triple
jump" (PDF p. 112, printed p. 95). Men's long jump snatch correlations ran 6.5-7.3m level
(PDF p. 103, printed p. 86). The half squat with barbell transferred even more
consistently — all levels, both sexes, in high jump and pole vault (PDF p. 112, printed
p. 95).

**Women's pole vault exception.** The single strongest correlation for women pole vaulters
was not the short-run-up vault: it was the 60m run from blocks (0.856, 0.886), above the
short-run-up vault itself (0.788, 0.865) (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94) — an exception to
"short-run-up is the single strongest exercise across event types" worth carrying alongside
that generalization. (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closer to the competitive event than general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises —
but this connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation, and
the internal high-jump contradiction above shows the pattern is not clean even on the
author's own numbers. **Inference:** the high jump's approach and takeoff (curved run,
back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a straight-line sprint that

principle of the “unity of general and specialized preparation”.  If we move away from 
multi-structure, multi-function and multi-system physical exercises, it becomes clear that 
even in the 1960-1970’s, general preparation means were practically not used in the 
training of athletes having different sports qualifications.  
 
In order to not make unsubstantiated statements we will present several examples.  In the 
training of jumpers and throwers, short distance runs were relegated to general 
preparation means.  But this is a specialized-preparatory exercise, in as much as their 
execution develops the speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor and extensor muscles that 
are actively involved in all throws and jumps.  Regardless of this, short distance runs are 
repeated in jumps as they are one of the structural components of the competitive event 
as for example, in the long jump.  Also, in the training of sprinters, jumpers and throwers 
how is it possible to execute a barbell clean or half squat with the barbell as a means of 
general preparation if these muscle groups participate in executing the competitive 
exercise?  The discussion here is related to the flexors and extensors of the legs. 
 
Even more surprising is the classification of middle and long distance running which has 
an aerobic effect, as a means of general preparation.  In execution of the workloads 
coordinated body systems (the nerve-muscle, respiratory, heart-circulatory, and other 
systems) participate even without taking into consideration running technique.   
 
No matter how we “specialize” the means of general preparation, no one and nowhere in 
sports practice is it possible to escape the negative effects when there is development of 
unnecessary muscle groups in one or another sports discipline, especially in speed-
strength events.  Specialists in the sprints, jumps and throws know that extreme 
development of speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor muscles shows up negatively on 
the physical ability of the leg extensors. 
 
This finding is related to the technique of executing the competitive exercise.  Also, 
extreme development of arm strength in the training of a hammer thrower leads to a 
as a whole or their separate parts.  Other muscle groups take part in 
the work being done.  The functional systems of the body are 
activated but do not ensure an increase in results in the competitive 
exercise.  General preparatory exercises (also known as general 
physical preparation (GPP) appear as a means of all-round 
development of the individual, and have a positive influence on 
increasing the general level of work ability and coordination.  At the 
same time, their use with other forms of exercises serve the flow of 
the restorative processes (active rest).

exercise is throwing the 7.26kg competition shot in a meet. The author does not give a clean
example of a general-preparatory exercise for a thrower in the excerpted chapters; he
argues most things coaches call "general" for speed-strength athletes (short runs,
barbell lifts, even aerobic running) are misclassified (PDF p. 24; see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so this entry does not invent one.

    14	# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
    17	preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
    18	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
    19	[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
    20	improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
    21	conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
    22	specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
    23	necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
    24	well as for carrying out restorative measures." He adds two further, separately unhedged
    25	and untested claims (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158): first, that future methods may "widen
    26	the range of transfer with the specialized-preparatory exercises to the competitive and
    27	specialized-developmental exercises"; second, that specialized-preparatory exercises "can
    28	appear as 'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the
    29	transfer to the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves.
    30	Neither claim is tested in the excerpted text.
    31	
    32	**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the "stimulational factors... on the brain
    33	level" phrase itself, which the author does not unpack further. This is the author's own
    34	explicit hedge against a naive misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data
    35	shows no further correlation, therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns
    36	against). **Inference:** the "stimulational factor" idea reads as an echo of the "tie-in
    37	effect" from Chapter 1 (see [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]),
    38	where an exercise with no measurable direct effect nonetheless enabled other exercises'
    39	gains — but the author does not himself connect these two passages.
    40	
    41	**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
    42	any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
    43	athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
    44	keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance. **Eric's baseline:**
    45	this is consistent with residual strength retention and the roughly-30-day residual
    46	training effect windows this library already tracks (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and
    47	power") and for its restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.
    48	
    49	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
    50	practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
    51	separately tested finding in its own right; his two forward-looking claims (widened
    52	transfer range, "stimulational factors") are untested speculation, not data. **Population:**
    53	native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
    54	from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
    55	printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — the same
    56	population as the ceiling-effect claims this heuristic responds to. Applying "keep it for
    57	maintenance, not for further gains" to
    58	a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
    59	directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
    60	volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
    61	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
    62	training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
    63	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
    64	the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
    65	different reasoning.
    66	
    67	**Example** — **Inference:** a discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
    68	distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
    69	and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
    70	weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
    71	than dropping squats from the program entirely.
    72	
    73	**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
    74	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
    75	a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
    76	the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
    77	echoes.

In conclusion, it should be noted that the search for new methods of constructing cycles 
of sports form development coincides with the appearance of studies in which it has been 
substantiated that the means of general preparation can create the “base”, “foundation”, 
for increasing results in the competitive events only in the training of low level athletes 
[57, 266].  The transfer of trainedness from general preparation exercises to the 
competitive is absent in high level athletes.  If a certain number of general preparation 
means are used by then, it is for carrying out general warm up and restoration [57, 266].   
 
At this time, more athletes have begun to move away from using the stage method of 
    14	# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk opens by naming the competitive exercise itself as the
    17	benchmark: determining an exercise's influence on the competitive exercise, "which in all
    18	track and field events, is the most important test" (PDF p. 68, printed p. 51). He then
    19	splits the other tests used to study training transfer into two families (PDF pp. 68-69,
    20	printed pp. 51-52):
    21	- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
    22	  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
    23	  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
    24	  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
    25	  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
    26	  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
    27	  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
    28	- **Specialized tests**: "In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very
    29	  similar" and "Each event in this group has its own specific tests" (PDF p. 68, printed
    30	  p. 51) — tests unique to each event's specific demands (lighter/heavier implements in
    31	  throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
    32	  events).
    33	
    34	Of tests generally, he singles out reliability separately from the general/specialized
    35	split: the reliability of tests built from **specialized-developmental exercises** "has
    36	already been shown," while the reliability of tests using general-preparatory and
    37	specialized-preparatory exercises "still have not been fully confirmed. This will be
    38	tightened up in the near future." (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52.)
    39	
    40	**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
    41	asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
    42	citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
    43	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
    44	sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
    45	exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
    46	from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.
    47	
    48	**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, treat the competitive
    49	exercise itself as the single most important test (PDF p. 68, printed p. 51). Below that,
    50	prioritize tests that are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the
    51	competitive skill under altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power
    52	tests when the goal is tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic
    53	tests (snatch, squat, vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which
    54	the author himself says have reliability "not fully confirmed" even though they are
    55	common practice.
    56	
    57	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
    58	methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
    59	without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
    60	(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
    61	no reference number here). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field
    62	athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles
    63	plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
    64	football, not team sport; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov
    65	jump, etc.) reflect that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based
    66	options. **Inference:** applying the general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own
    67	battery design (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") is this entry's own
    68	extension in terms of which specific tests to pick, and the claim that the underlying
    69	logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement) is "directly portable" is this
    70	entry's judgment, not the author's.
    71	
    72	**Example** — **Inference:** for a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this
    73	framework would be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route
    74	run against a lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump),
    75	while a "general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
    76	position group.
    77	
    78	**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
    79	this test-selection framework is built on.

14	# Bondarchuk Rejects the "Transfer at Start/Middle/End" Timing Model: Transfer Happens Over the Duration of a Stage, and Only Given Succession
    15	
    16	**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
    17	reversed the author's own conclusion. Bondarchuk first lists three situations "one can
    18	encounter" **in sports practice** — not his own proposal — for when the achieved level
    19	from a previous stage/block might transfer into the next one (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
    20	18-19):
    21	1. Transfer at the **start** of the next stage/block (the earlier result can then decrease,
    22	   increase, or hold — it already did its job).
    23	2. Transfer in the **middle** of the next stage/block (the earlier level must be actively
    24	   maintained, not allowed to drop, while the next stage's exercises are built).
    25	3. Transfer at the **end** of the next stage/block (the earlier level must be held all the
    26	   way through).
    27	He also gives the one method he says is known for maintaining an earlier level: keep the
    28	earlier stage's exercises in the program at much-reduced volume through the following
    29	stage rather than dropping them (PDF p. 36, printed p. 19, Figure 1: the stage-complex
    30	method's schematic for holding general-preparatory results into the specialized-
    31	preparatory stage).
    32	
    33	He then **rejects this three-situation timing model as his own conclusion**: "we came to
    34	the conclusion that the transfer of the achieved level of physical and other capabilities
    35	at the end of each of the previous stage, block, takes place **not at the beginning,
    36	middle or end** of each of the following stages, blocks, **but over the duration of
    37	them**" (PDF p. 37, printed p. 20, opened as an image to confirm the text layer). And this
    38	transfer is conditional, not automatic: "the transfer of training can occur only in those
    39	situations in which, over the duration of the entire stages, blocks, a succession is
    40	observed in the methods of training used. The exercises used appear to be those that...
    41	lengthen or shorten the time of entering into a state of sports form in the competitive
    42	exercise. These are mainly specialized-developmental exercises. If a succession in the use
    43	of the exercises does not exist, then transfer is not observed" (PDF pp. 37-38, printed
    44	pp. 20-21). Excluding specialized-developmental and competitive exercises for more than
    45	3-4 weeks under the variational method causes a real loss of the previously achieved level
    46	(PDF p. 38, printed p. 21).
    47	
    48	Separately, he distinguishes two broader modes across an entire multi-stage cycle:
    49	**"distant" transfer** (entering sports form in one exercise class first, other classes
    50	only later) versus **"current" (flowing) transfer** (all exercise classes reach sports
    51	form together, via a consistent, unbroken mix of exercise classes running throughout every
    52	stage). Current transfer is associated with variational, combinational, and complex
    53	methods of cycle construction; distant transfer with the stricter stage/block methods —
    54	but current transfer is **also** observed on stages of general preparation and in blocks
    55	of physical preparation when using the stage and block methods themselves (PDF p. 42,
    56	printed p. 25), so "distant transfer only happens under stage/block methods" is
    57	incomplete. (PDF pp. 41-42, 66-67, printed pp. 24-25, 49-50.)
    58	
    59	**Why it works** — No physiological mechanism is offered for either the succession
    60	requirement or the current/distant distinction; this is a purely descriptive,
    61	practice-derived model the author says he arrived at by observation ("we came to the
    62	conclusion that..."), with no cited independent verification or controlled comparison in
    63	the excerpted text. **Inference:** the "current transfer" mode maps loosely onto what
    64	Western periodization literature calls concurrent or conjugate training (train all
    65	qualities across the whole cycle, in varying proportions) versus "distant transfer"
    66	mapping onto strict block/linear periodization (sequential single-quality phases) — a
    67	connection this passage does not make itself.
    68	
    69	**When to apply** — Use the succession rule, not the three-situation timing model, as the
    70	lens for a periodization complaint: if an athlete's speed or strength level noticeably
    71	drops during a technical or in-season phase, ask whether the program has broken the
    72	succession of specialized-developmental/competitive exercises linking the stages (per the
    73	book's actual conclusion), not simply whether it labelled the drop-off "start," "middle,"
    74	or "end" transfer. **Inference:** mapped onto Eric's baseline, in-season programming at
    75	Baylor follows "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than dropping strength work
    76	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
    77	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) — that is one practical way of keeping the
    78	succession Bondarchuk's conclusion requires, though the course material does not use his
    79	terminology and this mapping is this entry's own, not the source's.
    80	
    81	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested** for the succession conclusion itself:
    82	it is the author's own unverified synthesis from practical observation, not tested against
    83	a control condition or independently replicated, and the book gives no citation trail for
    84	it (unusual for this chapter, which otherwise cites bracketed references throughout).
    85	**Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification,
    86	data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results
    87	(PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport.
    88	Applying the succession rule to a much shorter college football in-season/off-season
    89	calendar is Inference.
    90	
    91	**Example** — **Inference:** a discus thrower doing a strength-emphasis GPP block followed
    92	by a technical/competition block keeps the strength exercises in the program at reduced
    93	volume through the technical block (per PDF p. 36's maintenance schematic) rather than

    95	earlier strength work "pays off" during the technical block is not which of the three

    97	links the two blocks.

**Related** — [[heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]]:
    16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
    17	between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
    18	- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
    19	  ref [223]; the source text misgenders Thorndike as "She"): transfer between two
    20	  activities happens only when there is "some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of
    21	  elements" between them. No shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
    22	  **Inference:** this entry glosses "elements" as muscle groups, coordination structure,
    23	  and biomechanics; the source itself only says "concurrence (identicalness) of elements"
    24	  without spelling those out in this passage.
    25	- **Generalists** (their views "were formed during the years from 1940-1960," per the
    26	  text — not stated to have been dominant): argue for the "unity of general and
    27	  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
    28	  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
    29	  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
    30	  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
    31	  specialized-preparation means (citing three refs, [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed
    32	  pp. 5-7.) As that revision took hold, the ratio of training time given to general vs.
    33	  specialized preparation shifted: "If, at the beginning the correlation between the time
    34	  spent on general and specialized preparation was expressed in a 3:1 ratio, it later
    35	  changed in favor of an increased number of specialized preparation means" (PDF p. 23,
    36	  printed p. 6).
    37	- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
    38	  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
    39	  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
    40	  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
    41	  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
    42	  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions. He also names a deficiency in
    43	  their theory: because holistics indirectly call for training the cardiovascular/
    44	  respiratory systems first to drive neuromuscular adaptation, "the athlete enters the
    45	  highest training state in non-specific exercises at the start and only after this...
    46	  enters a state of sports form in the specific exercises," and "the level of trainedness
    47	  decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized exercises"
    48	  (PDF p. 28, printed p. 11). He notes that jumps, throws, and hurdles coaches agree with
    49	  the holistics on developing physical capacity before technique, formalized as the
    50	  "block" method of separate physical- and technical-preparation blocks (crediting
    51	  Y.V. Verkhoshansky, ref [49]) — but then calls the form/content split underlying it "a
    52	  theoretical and practical error... since they are united in all of their displays" (PDF
    53	  p. 28, printed p. 11); his answer to that error is the principle of conjugated training
    54	  effects (see [[principle--conjugated-training-effects]]). (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp.
    55	  9-11.)
    56	
    57	**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
    58	section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
    59	he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
    60	the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
    61	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
    62	and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
    63	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
    64	the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
    65	via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).
    66	
    67	**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
    68	S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
    69	positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
    70	selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
    71	competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
    72	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`). **Inference:** that is functionally a
    73	generalist-then-specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives
    74	Eric's course material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist
    75	sequencing debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.
    76	
    77	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
    78	literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
    79	scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
    80	exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond three bracketed reference numbers
    81	([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign
    82	track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
    83	Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
    84	printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. Extending any of the three views to football
    85	programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
    86	passage states.
    87	
    88	**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
    89	taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was revised "with time" once
    90	high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past a certain
    91	qualification level (PDF p. 23, printed p. 6; the passage does not give a specific decade
    92	for the revision). **Inference:** the Chapter 2 ceiling-effect data in
    93	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] is a plausible empirical echo of this
    94	revision, though the revision text itself cites refs [34, 57, 182], not those tables.
    95	
    96	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
    97	staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
    98	[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
    99	uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

    46	  enters a state of sports form in the specific exercises," and "the level of trainedness
    47	  decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized exercises"
    48	  (PDF p. 28, printed p. 11). He notes that jumps, throws, and hurdles coaches agree with
    49	  the holistics on developing physical capacity before technique, formalized as the
    50	  "block" method of separate physical- and technical-preparation blocks (crediting
    51	  Y.V. Verkhoshansky, ref [49]) — but then calls the form/content split underlying it "a
    52	  theoretical and practical error... since they are united in all of their displays" (PDF
    53	  p. 28, printed p. 11); his answer to that error is the principle of conjugated training
    54	  effects (see [[principle--conjugated-training-effects]]). (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp.
    55	  9-11.)
    56	
    57	**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
    58	section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
    59	he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
    60	the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
    61	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
    62	and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
    63	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
    64	the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
    65	via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).
    66	
    67	**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
    68	S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
    69	positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
    70	selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
    71	competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
    72	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`). **Inference:** that is functionally a
    73	generalist-then-specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives
    74	Eric's course material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist
    75	sequencing debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.
    76	
    77	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
    78	literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
    79	scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
    80	exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond three bracketed reference numbers
    81	([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign
    82	track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
    83	Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
    84	printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. Extending any of the three views to football
    85	programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
    86	passage states.
    87	
    88	**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
    89	taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was revised "with time" once
    90	high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past a certain
    91	qualification level (PDF p. 23, printed p. 6; the passage does not give a specific decade
    92	for the revision). **Inference:** the Chapter 2 ceiling-effect data in
    93	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] is a plausible empirical echo of this
    94	revision, though the revision text itself cites refs [34, 57, 182], not those tables.
    95	
    96	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
    97	staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
    98	[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
    99	uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

14	# The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects: Physical Preparation and Technique Must Coincide
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Physical-ability development and technical-mastery development should
    17	be trained so they "coincide and correspond to the competitive exercise according to
    18	their basic characteristics" rather than as separate tracks. Bondarchuk attributes the
    19	principle to Soviet head coach/scientist V.M. Dyachkov in the 1960s (ref [81]; PDF p. 28,
    20	printed p. 11), and notes it was later "modified by **other specialists** who called it
    21	dynamic correspondence and the principle of resolving motor actions. [157]." The text does
    22	not name who coined the term "dynamic correspondence"; the bracketed ref [157] attaches to
    23	the sentence as a whole, and the very next sentence separately credits U.V. Menkhin [157]
    24	with a specific extension: "the conjugate principle should affect not only the competitive
    25	event, but all the specialized activity as a whole." (PDF p. 29, printed p. 12.) Using gymnastics as
    26	Menkhin's example, the best conjugation requires five things at once: (1) motor qualities
    27	localized to the right muscle groups, (2) motor qualities matching the biodynamic demands
    28	of the skill, (3) transfer into the most common forms of motor activity used for learning
    29	technique, (4) enough work capacity to repeat the skill reliably across a long
    30	competition, and (5) transfer into the competitive combination itself. (PDF p. 29,
    31	printed p. 12.) Bondarchuk says he used this same conjugate principle to build his own
    32	"principle of all-round specialized preparation" (ref [265]): mostly specialized-
    33	preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises, general preparation only for warm-up
    34	and restoration, with each training cycle needing "new" and progressively stronger
    35	special exercises to keep producing adaptation. (PDF p. 30, printed p. 13.)
    36	
    37	**Why it works** — The author gives no explicit physiological mechanism here beyond the
    38	form-and-content unity idea inherited from the holistics critique in the prior section
    39	(see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]): training physical qualities
    40	and technique as artificially separate tracks is, in his view, a "theoretical and
    41	practical error" because they are "united in all of their displays." **Inference:** this
    42	reads as an early, narrower cousin of the ten-dimension specificity logic in
    43	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining) — both argue that an
    44	exercise's value depends on matching several specific parameters to the target skill, not
    45	just training "strength" or "technique" in isolation.
    46	
    47	**When to apply** — Use as a check when a program trains strength/power work and skill
    48	work in completely separate blocks with no attempt to match them: ask whether the
    49	strength work is being selected (per Menkhin's five criteria) to actually support the
    50	target skill's muscle groups, biodynamics, and movement pattern, not just "get stronger in
    51	general." **Eric's baseline:** the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
    52	is credited there to Verkhoshansky (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
    53	and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`; `week1-lecture.md p.34`).
    54	Bondarchuk's text is compatible with that credit, not in conflict with it: it names no one
    55	specifically as coining "dynamic correspondence," only "other specialists" with ref [157]
    56	(Menkhin) attached to the sentence. **Inference:** the course's Verkhoshansky attribution
    57	is the standard one in Western coaching literature; confirm against Supertraining's own
    58	Chapter 4.3 (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` in the Supertraining staging folder) before
    59	treating "dynamic correspondence" as a single-author concept in any future entry.
    60	
    61	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
    62	reading of Dyachkov's and Menkhin's Soviet-era proposals, cited only by bracketed
    63	reference number, not independently verified in this ingest. The five-component
    64	gymnastics example is Menkhin's, imported by Bondarchuk into track and field without
    65	restating it for that context; applying it to a specific football exercise-selection
    66	decision is Inference. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes
    67	of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
    68	published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
    69	football, not team sport. (Menkhin's own illustrative scheme is drawn from gymnastics, an
    70	example, not this book's tested population.)
    71	
    72	**Example** — **Inference:** a football strength coach picking a trap-bar deadlift
    73	variation for a linebacker should, per this principle, be asking not just "does this build
    74	leg strength" but whether the pull's force direction, joint angles, and muscle-work regime
    75	actually match the demands of a linebacker's competitive movement — the same "coincide and
    76	correspond" test Bondarchuk describes for track and field exercise selection.
    77	
    78	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
    79	staging) — cites Verkhoshansky's Dynamic Correspondence by name; flag the Dyachkov/Menkhin
    80	vs. Verkhoshansky attribution question there too if that entry is revisited.
    81	[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] — the holistics' form-and-content
    82	unity critique this principle is offered to resolve.
