14	# Correlation Can Hide a "Tie-In" Exercise That Is Actually Doing the Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
    17	analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
    18	interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
    19	5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
    20	reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives one
    21	illustrative case, which he frames as typical rather than isolated ("we will address only
    22	one of the situations which frequently arise in the process of doing experimental studies
    23	on this problem," PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54): a training session using three
    24	exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results improved in A and C but
    25	not in B. "The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B,
    26	which made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.
    27	Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had
    28	on exercise A or C. Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not
    29	effective." A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained only A and C — and this time
    30	**neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation: exercise B had a "tie-in
    31	effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even though B itself showed no
    32	measurable within-exercise result. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)
    33	
    34	**Why it works** — The author's own explanation for why a single pairwise correlation can
    35	mislead: "the direction and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the
    36	integration of activity in the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions
    37	between the excitatory-inhibitory processes" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53) — this is also his
    38	stated reason for insisting on a minimum of 5-6 indices per athlete group rather than
    39	single pairwise comparisons. Beyond that stated reason, he defers the tie-in mechanism
    40	itself to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." **Inference:** the
    41	described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
    42	blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
    43	pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
    44	between two *other* exercises — this structural-blindness framing is this entry's own
    45	reading, not the author's stated point.
    46	
    47	**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
    48	exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
    49	result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
    50	of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing.
    51	**Inference:** this is a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut
    52	what isn't working" is a common simplification heuristic that this example directly
    53	complicates — that practical framing is this entry's own, not the author's.
    54	
    55	**Method (applies to every Chapter 2 correlation entry in this book folder):**
    56	questionnaires from native (USSR) and foreign athletes of mixed qualification, carried out
    57	over four Olympic cycles, plus published individual results (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp.
    58	vii-viii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); "a positive interrelationship between exercises begins
    59	at 0.349" (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59; 0.423 for women's pole vault, PDF p. 111, printed
    60	p. 94); and the data is restricted to training systems **without** steroid use, because
    61	steroid use raises results across all exercises used and not used, masking which exercise
    62	actually drove the transfer (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. vii-viii).
    63	
    64	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This finding rests on one worked
    65	example, with no stated sample size, no statistical test, and no independent replication
    66	in the excerpted text — it is presented by the author himself as an open question for
    67	future research ("we believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this
    68	interaction"), not a settled result, even though he frames the underlying situation as one
    69	that "frequently arise[s]." Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise
    70	combination has a tie-in effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what
    71	pairwise correlation studies (including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect.
    72	Exercises A/B/C are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is
    73	nothing concrete to generalize from besides the logical structure of the example and the
    74	Method note above.
    75	
    76	**Example** — **Inference:** a strength coach who drops an unweighted plyometric drill
    77	from a sprint-training session because the drill's own jump-height numbers aren't
    78	improving might, per this heuristic, want to check whether removing it also flattens the
    79	sprint-speed gains the program was otherwise seeing — the drill could be a tie-in exercise
    80	even though its own metric looks stagnant.
    81	
    82	**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific correlation blind spot;
    83	flag for cross-reference if a future ingest (e.g., a sports-statistics or research-methods
    84	source) covers interaction effects or mediation more formally.

    14	# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
    17	take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
    18	though some individuals take "4-7 and even 8 months" (PDF p. 39, printed p. 22). A
    19	general-preparation stage/block can only function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the
    20	following specialized stage if it lasts at least as long as that individual's own
    21	sports-form development timeline. He gives his own worked numbers for how this plays out:
    22	in a single-cycle training year, the general-preparation stage runs "on the average, three
    23	months," long enough to let most athletes actually enter sports form in it; in a two-cycle
    24	year, the second general-preparation stage shrinks to "4-6 weeks," and in a three-cycle
    25	year to "2-3 weeks" — both too short for athletes to "have time to enter into full sports
    26	form in the exercises used." (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) He gives a
    27	worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
    28	15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
    29	entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
    30	needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
    31	general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
    32	(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
    33	their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
    34	endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
    35	stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
    36	transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
    37	of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
    38	(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
    39	23-25.)
    40	
    41	**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
    42	entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
    43	duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
    44	that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
    45	training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
    46	developmental phase in itself.
    47	
    48	**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
    49	"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
    50	phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
    51	in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
    52	it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
    53	retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
    54	days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
    55	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
    56	distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
    57	developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.
    58	
    59	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month ("4-7 and even 8 month")
    60	sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
    61	specific citation in the excerpted pages. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track
    62	and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
    63	Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
    64	printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
    65	calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
    66	sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
    67	a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
    68	adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
    69	is more portable than the specific duration numbers.
    70	
    71	**Example** — **Inference:** a 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very
    72	unlikely to produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the
    73	Bondarchuk sense; it functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training
    74	stress, and should be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building
    75	a real strength or conditioning "base."
    76	
    77	**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
    78	model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
    79	(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
    80	duration question applies to.

14	# Three Types of Training Transfer, Plus "Indifferent" (Double-Effect) Transfer
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three types of training transfer (PDF p. 31, printed
    17	p. 14):
    18	- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
    19	- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
    20	  another.
    21	- **Neutral**: no measurable effect either way.
    22	
    23	He then adds a fourth term, drawn from outside literature, not presented as his own
    24	addition: "In the specialized literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent'
    25	transfer." He returns to it separately: "In addition to these three noted forms of
    26	training transfer we more rarely meet with indifferent transfer" — **indifferent transfer
    27	is the double-effect case**, not a synonym for neutral. It shows up "especially... when
    28	training high level athletes who use a whole complex of different exercises," and can have
    29	"a double effect on one another": a positive effect on one dimension and a negative effect
    30	on another at the same time. Example: heavier-implement throws can be "positive... on
    31	increasing the functional capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the
    32	technique," and "there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the use
    33	of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]) — with increased strength, "a negative change in
    34	the process of executing separate elements as well as the entire movement as a whole"
    35	[152]. (PDF p. 31, printed p. 14.)
    36	
    37	Bondarchuk gives a specific worked example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/
    38	anaerobic running in general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory
    39	function but worsened walking technique [94] — a positive-physiological/negative-technical
    40	double effect. He also gives a remedy: walkers can avoid the negative influence "by using
    41	mainly specialized-developmental and competitive exercises"; in other running events,
    42	hurdles, and throws, coaches can select among exercises so "there would be more good ones
    43	rather than poor ones," which "makes it possible to eliminate the negative influence on
    44	technique in several weekly cycles." (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)
    45	
    46	**Why it works** — For the three-way split, Bondarchuk gives no mechanism; he presents it
    47	as received terminology. For the double-effect (indifferent) case specifically, he does
    48	give an explanation: "The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent
    49	transfer) is most frequently explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning,
    50	interfere with the unity between form and content" (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15) — the
    51	same form-and-content framing used against the holistics' block method (see
    52	[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]). **Note on scope:** Chapter 1's
    53	earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements" (PDF p. 20, printed
    54	p. 3; see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk
    55	as the basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by
    56	him to this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim
    57	that link was Bondarchuk's own.
    58	
    59	**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new exercise:
    60	is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect (indifferent)**
    61	where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
    62	technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
    63	illustration. **Inference:** flagging any high-volume general-conditioning block for a
    64	technical, timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect
    65	risk is this entry's own extension of the walking case, not something the passage states
    66	for those sports; the author's own remedy (favor specialized-developmental/competitive
    67	exercises, or bias exercise selection toward "good" over "poor" options) applies whichever
    68	sport is in question.
    69	
    70	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
    71	implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
    72	technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
    73	reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
    74	**Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification,
    75	data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results
    76	(PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport.
    77	Extending "double effect" reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint
    78	mechanics) is Inference, plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.
    79	
    80	**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
    81	GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
    82	effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
    83	reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
    84	example here.
    85	
    86	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
    87	staging) — **Inference:** a plausible mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases could
    88	run through (mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions), not a link the source
    89	itself draws.
Types of Training Transfer 
 
There are three types of training transfer: positive, negative, and neutral.  In the 
specialized literature it is also possible to find “indifferent” transfer. 
 
Positive transfer of training means that there is a positive effect of one exercise on 
another.  In other words, with an increase in the sports result in one exercise, a parallel 
increase takes place in another exercise. 
 
In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the 
exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a 
simultaneous decrease in other exercises. 
 
In neutral transfer of training there is no increase or decrease in sports achievement.  The 
training does not show any affect on another training. 
 
In addition to these three noted forms of training transfer we more rarely meet with 
indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a 
whole complex of different exercises, and depends on their coordination structure and 
strength of their influence.  At the present time, the interrelationships between the 
exercises are complex and unpredictable, and they may have a double effect on one 
another. For example, there may be a positive affect on increasing the functional 
capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the technique an exercise [92].  
In track and field, there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the 
use of heavier implements [18, 152]. In these cases, with an increase in strength, there is 
a negative change in the process of executing separate elements as well the entire 
movement as a whole [152]. 
 
The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent transfer) is most frequently

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing, but Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin and hammer, Bondarchuk tests four
strength exercises: snatch, power clean, squat with the barbell on the shoulders, and
bench press. Hammer throwers are the exception for the bench press, "as this exercise is
not used by most of them in the process of training" (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116). The
exercises show a positive transfer to the competitive throw **in most event and sex
groups** (exception: javelin, see below), but **only up to a specific result level for
each exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive
improvement disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer was
observed up to 45-50m (men) and 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m;
bench press extended furthest, to 55-60m (men) and 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch
reached 60-65m, power clean 65-70m, squat 60-65m (men); in women, the cumulative effect
was fixed "at the level of 45-60m" for these exercises (the women's competitive hammer is
4kg, Table 84, PDF p. 130, so these distances are not comparable with the men's). In shot put, snatch
reached 17-18m (men) and 15-16m (women), power clean 14-15m (men) and "14-25m" (women; a
probable typo in the printed text, since the source has a real text layer rather than
OCR, so this is either a source misprint or an unusually wide band), squat 19-20m (men)
and 17-18m (women), bench 18-19m (men) and 19-20m (women). **In javelin, the pattern
breaks**: snatch and power clean both reached 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was
no correlation seen" for either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch reached
60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, and the squat showed "no cumulative transfer
effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-134, printed pp. 116-117.)

**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59). **Inference:** the
result levels above are the qualification bands where the correlations clear that
threshold; this passage gives the bands, not the coefficients.

Bondarchuk's aggregate summary at the close of the book's data chapters:
"specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in the sports
result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery. Further on, they
do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) Later in the same throws
section he adds that "the leading throwers (world and Olympic champions and world record
holders) do not always have the best absolute results in the specialized-preparatory
exercises" (PDF p. 139, printed p. 122). **Inference:** this fits the ceiling: being the
best thrower does not require the best strength numbers.

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for why the ceiling occurs at these
levels. **Inference:** it is consistent with a diminishing-returns pattern: general
strength predicts performance at lower levels of mastery, but once strength is no longer
the limiting factor, technical and specialized qualities (captured better by the
specialized-developmental exercises in
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) become the binding
constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this interpretation.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a thrower's (or other power athlete's)
emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward specialized-developmental
work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the athlete's **competitive
result** passes the band where the cumulative effect ends for their event (the ceilings
above are competition-distance bands, not strength-load thresholds), rather than chasing
strength PRs as the main lever for competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** These are group-level ceilings; the
author cautions against reading them as fixed for every individual: "if we take into
consideration individual and not group indices in the above mentioned strength exercises,
then it is very possible that in individual cases we will see the cumulative effect
appearing on different levels of sports mastery for each athlete. They will be very
individualized. It may show that in women it can be even higher than in men" (PDF p. 135,
printed p. 118). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of
mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport. The four lifts are the snatch, power clean, barbell squat and
bench press, with no stated depth or technique standards. The exact result-level bands are
specific to this book's dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry
does NOT mean "stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached; see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's
statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for maintenance and
restoration. Applying this ceiling logic to a football strength athlete (for example an
offensive lineman) is Inference: there is no football data here, and a lineman's
"competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured throw.

**Example** — **Inference:** a male discus thrower already throwing past 50-55m should
not, on this data, expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus distance;
continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and technical
work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with strength work
maintained rather than chased. Per the individualisation caveat above, an individual
athlete may meet the ceiling at a different distance than the group figure.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]: the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]]: what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's words.
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]]: the parallel, even more limited
ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the Glossary is
unsigned and contains lines in the translator's voice: "In the U.S., these terms are most
often used interchangeably" (Means and Methods entry) and "The physical education
discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the Russian literature than in the
U.S." (Physical Education entry), plus "This is a unique term that has no analogy in the
English language" (Motor Analyzer entry), all PDF p. 13, printed p. xii. Per the task
brief's rule, a translator (Yessis) voice is not the author's. Treat the definitions below as
**the translated edition's**, possibly Yessis's own glosses; Bondarchuk's own usage of these
terms is visible in Chapter 1-2 prose instead (for example PDF p. 24, printed p. 7; PDF p. 62,
printed p. 45, "we did not take exercises from the general developmental group"). Do not
cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future entry without that caveat. The Glossary's
own abbreviation is "SPP" for **Specialized Exercises** ("Also known as specialized
physical preparation (SPP)," PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii), a different label than
"specialized-preparatory," which the Glossary does not itself abbreviate. For general
preparatory exercises the Glossary gives "GPP" itself. It never abbreviates
specialized-developmental exercises or competitive exercises as "SDE" or "CE"; those
abbreviations below are this entry's own shorthand, not the book's:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises ("GPP", the Glossary's own abbreviation: "also known as
  general physical preparation (GPP)", PDF p. 12, printed p. xi)**: "do not repeat
  the competitive actions as a whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part
  in the work being done. The functional systems of the body are activated but do not
  ensure an increase in results in the competitive exercise." Function: all-round
  development, work capacity, and active rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises ("SPE", this entry's abbreviation; the Glossary's own
  "SPP" label attaches to a related but separately defined "Specialized Exercises" entry,
  see above)**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the competitive actions as a whole
  or in their separate parts. However, they use similar muscle groups in their execution,"
  activating the functions and body systems the main movement depends on, with "identical
  or close to identical regimes of muscle work." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises ("SDE", this entry's abbreviation, not the
  Glossary's)**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts. In executing them,
  one and the same muscle groups participate, together with activation of similar systems
  and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the
  body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry into the state of sports form."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises ("CE", this entry's abbreviation, not the Glossary's)**: "the
  acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the athlete participates in competition,"
  executed either in actual competition or in training as a model/repeat of competitive
  conditions, easier or harder (this definition spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed
  pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts or body links: squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together: the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-factors-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). This entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is the book's own
classification scheme (see the voice note above on Glossary authorship). Two other sources
in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Russian-language
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field
athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles
plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport. The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (for example a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPE vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something the Glossary addresses.

**Example** — **Inference:** Bondarchuk's own placement of exercises across these classes,
for throwers: short distance runs are "a specialized-preparatory exercise", not general,
because they develop the leg flexor and extensor muscles used in all throws and jumps,
and he asks how "a barbell clean or half squat" can be general preparation when those
muscle groups take part in the competitive exercise (PDF p. 24, printed p. 7); lighter/heavier implement throws are
specialized-developmental (PDF p. 62, printed p. 45; PDF p. 69, printed p. 52); the competitive
exercise is throwing the 7.26kg competition shot in a meet. The author does not give a clean
example of a general-preparatory exercise for a thrower in the excerpted chapters; he
argues most things coaches call "general" for speed-strength athletes (short runs,
barbell lifts, even aerobic running) are misclassified (PDF p. 24; see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so this entry does not invent one.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault): the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-factors-general-to-competitive]]: the transfer
factors built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]:
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.

specialized-developmental exercises or competitive exercises as "SDE" or "CE"; those
abbreviations below are this entry's own shorthand, not the book's:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises ("GPP", the Glossary's own abbreviation: "also known as
  general physical preparation (GPP)", PDF p. 12, printed p. xi)**: "do not repeat
  the competitive actions as a whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part
  in the work being done. The functional systems of the body are activated but do not
  ensure an increase in results in the competitive exercise." Function: all-round
  development, work capacity, and active rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises ("SPE", this entry's abbreviation; the Glossary's own
  "SPP" label attaches to a related but separately defined "Specialized Exercises" entry,
  see above)**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the competitive actions as a whole
  or in their separate parts. However, they use similar muscle groups in their execution,"
  activating the functions and body systems the main movement depends on, with "identical
  or close to identical regimes of muscle work." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises ("SDE", this entry's abbreviation, not the
  Glossary's)**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts. In executing them,
  one and the same muscle groups participate, together with activation of similar systems
  and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the
  body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry into the state of sports form."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises ("CE", this entry's abbreviation, not the Glossary's)**: "the
  acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the athlete participates in competition,"
  executed either in actual competition or in training as a model/repeat of competitive
  conditions, easier or harder (this definition spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed
  pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts or body links: squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together: the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-factors-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). This entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is the book's own
classification scheme (see the voice note above on Glossary authorship). Two other sources
in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Russian-language
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field
athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles
plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport. The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (for example a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPE vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something the Glossary addresses.

[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so this entry does not invent one.
